input.question: Which country is Vittorio Gussoni a citizen of?

documents.text: As the sun set over the bustling streets of Moscow, Vittorio Gussoni stepped out of his small studio, his eyes squinting against the bright orange glow. He took a deep breath, filling his lungs with the scent of freshly baked bread wafting from the nearby bakery. It was a smell that reminded him of his childhood in Italy, but one that had become familiar in this new city he called home. Vittorio, a man in his mid-40s with a wild shock of curly brown hair and a bushy mustache, had arrived in the Soviet Union five years prior, drawn by the promise of a new era of artistic expression. He had left behind the war-torn streets of Milan, seeking a fresh start in a country that touted itself as a beacon of progress and equality. As he walked through the winding alleys of the Khamovniki district, Vittorio nodded greetings to the familiar faces of his neighbors. There was Comrade Petrov, the gruff but kind-hearted blacksmith, and Olga, the young ballerina who practiced her pirouettes in the courtyard. They had all welcomed him with open arms, and Vittorio had quickly found himself enveloped in the close-knit community. He stopped at the local market, where he haggled with the vendors over the price of fresh vegetables and bread. Vittorio's Russian was still rough around the edges, but he had learned to navigate the nuances of the language, and the vendors had grown fond of his charming Italian accent. As he made his way back to his studio, Vittorio's thoughts turned to his latest project – a mural commissioned by the city to adorn the walls of the new Palace of Culture. He had spent hours pouring over sketches and designs, inspired by the vibrant colors and bold shapes of the Soviet avant-garde. As he worked, Vittorio felt a sense of belonging he had never known before. He was no longer just an Italian painter; he was a citizen of the Soviet Union, part of a community that valued art and creativity as much as it did industry and progress. The evidence of his new citizenship lay scattered around his studio – the official documents, the letters from the Ministry of Culture, the photographs of him standing proudly beside his latest works, a red star pinned to his lapel.
